Let $V$ be an oriented finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension $n$, with Gram pairings on the exterior powers of [[def-gram-inner-product-on-kth-exterior-power]] and oriented unit volume form $\omega$ of [[def-oriented-unit-volume-form]]. For each degree $k$ with $0\le k\le n$, the **Hodge star**

$$\star:\Lambda^kV\longrightarrow\Lambda^{n-k}V$$

is the linear map characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\,\omega\qquad\text{for all }\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV.$$

Existence and uniqueness of $\star$ for every degree $0\le k\le n$ are proved in [[thm-hodge-star-exists-uniquely-and-has-the-orthonormal-basis-formula]], which discharges the well-definedness obligation recorded above.

Let $V$ be an oriented finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension $n$. For every degree $0\le k\le n$ there is a unique linear map $\star:\Lambda^kV\to\Lambda^{n-k}V$ satisfying

$$\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\,\omega\qquad\text{for all }\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV,$$

where $\omega$ is the oriented unit volume form of [[def-oriented-unit-volume-form]]. If $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis and $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_k\}$ has complement $I^c=\{i^c_1<\cdots<i^c_{n-k}\}$, let $\varepsilon_I$ be the sign of the permutation $(i_1,\ldots,i_k,i^c_1,\ldots,i^c_{n-k})\mapsto(1,\ldots,n)$; then

$$\star e_I=\varepsilon_I\,e_{I^c}.$$

On $\Lambda^kV$ of an oriented $n$-dimensional real inner product space, the Hodge star preserves the Gram pairing,

$$\langle\star\alpha,\star\beta\rangle=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle,$$

and satisfies

$$\star\circ\star=(-1)^{k(n-k)}\operatorname{id}_{\Lambda^kV}.$$

derivations.claim: Suppose $n=1$. Choose a unit vector $e_1$ and put $e_2=-Je_1$; then $g(e_1,e_2)=0$, $g(e_2,e_2)=1$, $Je_1=-e_2$, $Je_2=e_1$, and $\omega(e_1,e_2)=-g(Je_1,e_2)=g(e_2,e_2)=1$, so $\omega=e_1\wedge e_2$ is the positive unit volume form and $(e_1,e_2)$ is positively oriented. The basis $1,e_1,e_2,\omega$ of $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$ is orthonormal for $h$, and [F1] gives the star table $\star1=\omega$, $\star e_1=e_2$, $\star e_2=-e_1$, $\star\omega=1$. Hence $L(1)=\omega$ and $L$ kills $e_1,e_2,\omega$, while the adjoint $\Lambda$ satisfies $\Lambda\omega=1$ and kills $1,e_1,e_2$. Therefore $[L,\Lambda]=H$ is $-\mathrm{id}$, $0$, $0$, $\mathrm{id}$ on degrees $0,1,1,2$, that is $H=(k-1)\mathrm{id}$ on $\bigwedge^k$, and evaluating $HL-LH$ and $H\Lambda-\Lambda H$ on the four basis elements gives $[H,L]=2L$ and $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$. Evaluating the exponentials gives $W(1)=\omega$, $W(e_1)=e_1$, $W(e_2)=e_2$, $W(\omega)=-1$, while $J(1)=1$, $Je_1=-e_2$, $Je_2=e_1$, $J\omega=\omega$ give $\epsilon(0)J\star1=\omega$, $\epsilon(1)J\star e_1=e_1$, $\epsilon(1)J\star e_2=e_2$ and $\epsilon(2)J\star\omega=-1$; since both sides are complex linear, $W=\epsilon(k)J\star$ on $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ for $n=1$.

Let $V=V_1\oplus V_2$ with $V_1,V_2$ $g$-orthogonal and $J$-stable, oriented so that the positive volume form is $\operatorname{vol}_1\wedge\operatorname{vol}_2$; write $\omega_i=\omega|_{V_i}$, so $\omega=\omega_1+\omega_2$, and let $L_i,\Lambda_i,W_i,J_i$ be the corresponding operators on the factors. Under the linear isomorphism $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{1,\mathbb C}\otimes\bigwedge^\bullet V_{2,\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, $a\otimes b\mapsto a\wedge b$, a check on orthonormal wedge bases gives the tensor rules $h(a\wedge b,a'\wedge b')=h_1(a,a')h_2(b,b')$, $\star(a\wedge b)=(-1)^{\deg a\deg b}(\star_1a)\wedge(\star_2b)$ and $J(a\wedge b)=J_1a\wedge J_2b$ for homogeneous $a,a'$ and $b,b'$, the middle one being forced by the characterizing property [F1] and consistent with the isometry property [F2]. Consequently $L=L_1+L_2$, $\Lambda=\Lambda_1+\Lambda_2$ (the adjoint of a sum of operators acting on the two tensor factors is the sum of the adjoints), $H=H_1+H_2$ where $H_i=(\deg-n_i)\mathrm{id}$ on the $i$-th factor with $n_i=\dim V_i/2$, and $W=W_1W_2$, $J=J_1J_2$, because operators on the two factors commute. If the three commutator relations and the identity $W=\epsilon(k)J\star$ hold on both factors, then they hold on $V$: the commutator relations split termwise, and for homogeneous $a,b$ the identity gives $W(a\wedge b)=\epsilon(\deg a)\epsilon(\deg b)(J_1\star_1a)\wedge(J_2\star_2b)$, which equals $\epsilon(\deg a+\deg b)J\star(a\wedge b)$ because $\epsilon(m+\ell)=(-1)^{m\ell}\epsilon(m)\epsilon(\ell)$ and the sign $(-1)^{\deg a\deg b}$ of the star rule cancels against $(-1)^{m\ell}$. Splitting off a two-plane $W=\mathrm{span}(e_1,-Je_1)$ with $V_2=W^\perp$ and iterating the base case 1.1 proves the three relations of part 1 and the identity of part 4 for every $n\ge0$: the degenerate factor $V_2=0$ has $\bigwedge^\bullet V_2=\mathbb C$ in degree zero, where all operators are the identity or zero and the relations are immediate, and for $n=0$ both sides of $W=\epsilon(k)J\star$ are the identity on this one-dimensional space.

Let $u
e0$ be primitive of degree $t$, so $\Lambda u=0$. From $[L,\Lambda]=H$ and $H=(t+2r-n)\mathrm{id}$ on degree $t+2r$ we get, by induction on $r\ge0$, the recurrence $\Lambda L^ru=r(n-t-r+1)L^{r-1}u$: indeed $\Lambda L^{r}u=L\Lambda L^{r-1}u-(t+2(r-1)-n)L^{r-1}u$ and substituting the induction hypothesis for $r-1$ gives the claim. Iterating gives the displayed factorial formula. Let $N$ be the largest index with $L^Nu
e0$, which exists because $L^ru=0$ once $t+2r>2n$. Then $L^{N+1}u=0$, so the recurrence with $r=N+1$ gives $0=\Lambda L^{N+1}u=(N+1)(n-t-N)L^Nu$; since $N+1
e0$ and $L^Nu
e0$, we get $N=n-t$. Hence $n-t\ge0$, so no nonzero primitive element has degree $t>n$; moreover $L^{n-t}u
e0$ and $L^{n-t+1}u=0$, and all coefficients in the factorial formula are nonzero for $0\le s\le r\le n-t$.

Let $\alpha\in\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$. Since $\Lambda=L^*$ on the finite-dimensional space $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$, the image of $L:\bigwedge^{k-2}V_{\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ is the orthogonal complement of $\ker\Lambda$ on $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$, so $\alpha=u_0+L\alpha_1$ with $\Lambda u_0=0$ and $\alpha_1\in\bigwedge^{k-2}V_{\mathbb C}$. Inducting on $k$ (the cases $k=0$ and $k=1$ have no $L$-term) writes $\alpha=\sum_{r}L^ru_r$ with each $u_r$ primitive; terms with $\deg u_r>n$ vanish by step 3.1, and $L^ru_r=0$ when $r>n-\deg u_r$, equivalently $r<k-n$. Discarding these zero terms gives the stated range $r\ge\max(0,k-n)$. For uniqueness, suppose $\sum_{r=r_0}^{s}L^ru_r=0$ with each $u_r$ primitive and $u_s\ne0$. Put $c_r=r!(n-k+2r)!/(n-k+r)!$, which is a positive integer in this range. The factorial formula gives $\Lambda^sL^su_s=c_su_s$, while for $r<s$ it gives $\Lambda^sL^ru_r=\Lambda^{s-r}(c_ru_r)=0$ because $\Lambda u_r=0$; applying $\Lambda^s$ to the sum gives $c_su_s=0$, a contradiction. For the projections start with the fixed index $s=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$, allowing zero coefficients: $u_s=c_s^{-1}\Lambda^s\alpha$. Subtract $L^su_s$ and repeat with $s-1$ down to $\max(0,k-n)$. This expresses each $u_r$ by a fixed rational linear combination of compositions of $L,\Lambda$, without choices.

Choose a basis $(u_\alpha)$ of the direct sum $P=\bigoplus_jP^j$ of primitive spaces $P^j=\ker\Lambda\cap\bigwedge^jV_{\mathbb C}$, a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional spaces. By step 4.1 every element of $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$ has a unique expression as a finite sum of string elements $L^ru_\alpha$ with $0\le r\le n-\deg u_\alpha$; hence these string elements form a basis, and the string of $u_\alpha$ occupies each degree $t_\alpha,t_\alpha+2,\dots,2n-t_\alpha$. Fix $k\le n$ and let $t_\alpha=\deg u_\alpha$. Multiplication by $L^{n-k}$ sends the string element at position $r$ to position $r+n-k$, which is a valid position of the same string because $r+n-k\le n-t_\alpha$ follows from $k=t_\alpha+2r$; conversely position $r'$ of a degree-$2n-k$ element of the string is the image of $r=r'-(n-k)$ with $k=t_\alpha+2r\ge0$. On the direct sum of strings, $L^{n-k}$ is therefore a bijection from the degree-$k$ part onto the degree-$2n-k$ part, an isomorphism $L^{n-k}:\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^{2n-k}V_{\mathbb C}$. Similarly, $L^{n-k+1}L^ru_\alpha=L^{r+n-k+1}u_\alpha$ is zero exactly when $r=0$, and for $r\ge1$ it is a nonzero string element; expanding $u=\sum_{r\ge0,\alpha}c_{r,\alpha}L^ru_\alpha$ in degree $k$ and using basis independence, $L^{n-k+1}u=0$ forces $c_{r,\alpha}=0$ for every $r\ge1$, so $u=\sum_\alpha c_{0,\alpha}u_\alpha$ is primitive. The converse is step 3.1.

Since $J$ acts as $i$ on $V^{1,0}$ and $-i$ on $V^{0,1}$ and is multiplicative, $J=i^{p-q}$ on $\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$. Let $u\ne0$ be primitive of degree $k$ and type $(p,q)$, put $m=n-k\ge0$, and apply $W=\exp L\exp(-\Lambda)\exp L$ to $\exp(-L)u$: since $\Lambda u=0$ we get $W\exp(-L)u=\exp(L)\exp(-\Lambda)u=\exp(L)u$. Expanding $\exp(-L)u$ and comparing the components of degree $2n-k$, of which the left side has exactly $Wu$ (all other terms are mapped to lower degrees by $W$, which reverses the $H$-weight) and the right side exactly $L^mu/m!$, gives $Wu=L^mu/m!$. Substituting into the identity $Wu=\epsilon(k)J\star u$ of step 2.1 and applying $J^{-1}$, which acts on $L^mu$ by $i^{-(p-q)}=i^{q-p}$ because $L^mu$ has type $(p+m,q+m)$, gives $\star u=\epsilon(k)i^{q-p}L^mu/m!$, which is the displayed formula. For $n=0$ both sides are the identity and the formula is $*1=1$.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, and $k\ge0$, define
$$I_M^k:\Omega^k(M)\longrightarrow C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R),\qquad I_M^k(\omega)(\sigma)=\int_\sigma\omega.$$
On $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ this means $I_M^k(\omega)(c)=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$, a finite sum. In negative degrees $I_M^k$ is the zero map. Forms and the de Rham complex at a boundary use [[lem-the-de-rham-complex-and-pullback-extend-to-manifolds-with-boundary]]. No orientation of $M$ is required: the domain simplex has the specified orientation. The name integration cochain map is justified by [[thm-de-rham-integration-is-a-cochain-map]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, the inclusion of smooth into continuous real singular chains induces an isomorphism
$$H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$$
in every integer degree. This isomorphism is natural for smooth maps. The proof smooths only finitely many simplices at a time. For boundary targets it moves a finite compact set into the interior; it does not prescribe arbitrary boundary faces during smoothing.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

For negative $n$, the two groups are zero and the pairing is the zero map. Empty $X$ and zero $G$ also give zero evaluation. When $G$ is an $R$-module, the cohomology variable is $R$-linear and the integral homology variable is additive; an $R$-bilinear pairing instead uses chains and homology over $R$ with $R$-linear cochains. No representative-selection function is included in the definition.

The Kronecker rule $\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c)$ is independent of both cocycle and cycle representatives and is additive in both variables. For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^n(Y;G)$ and $z\in H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, it satisfies
$$\langle f^*\alpha,z\rangle=\langle\alpha,f_*z\rangle.$$
For a coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$, it satisfies $\langle u_*\alpha,z\rangle=u\langle\alpha,z\rangle$. The same representative-independence argument gives the $R$-bilinear pairing for $R$-linear cochains on chains over a commutative ring $R$.

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

The same lemma gives finitely many open-and-closed components $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ and the restriction isomorphism
$$H_n(M;R)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^k H_n(M,M\setminus M_j;R).$$
The summand on the right identifies with $H_n(M_j;R)$: apply [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] to remove the closed set $M\setminus M_j$, which is the entire open relative subspace. The resulting pair is $(M_j,\varnothing)$. Under this identification $[M]$ corresponds to the finite tuple of the component fundamental classes.

If the orientation is negated on one component, its new fundamental-class summand is the negative of its old one. Indeed restriction is linear, so the negative class restricts to $-\mu_x$ at all points of that component, and uniqueness in the compact-set lemma identifies it with the new class. The other component summands are unchanged. In characteristic two this negation can leave the orientation and class unchanged; no distinction between $\mu$ and $-\mu$ is imposed when they are equal.

For empty $M$ the fundamental class is $0$ in the zero homology group, with an empty direct sum. For $R=0$ the unique orientation gives the zero class. A compact zero-manifold has finitely many singleton components, and its fundamental zero-cycle has at each point the coefficient prescribed by its local module generator. The definition requires a supplied orientation and uses no AC or simultaneous choice of one orientation per component.

Fix a dimension $n\ge1$ and one generator $e_n$ of $H_n(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\};\mathbb Z)$. A smooth orientation on a boundaryless $n$-manifold determines an integral local-homology orientation by requiring each positive chart centred at $p$ to send its local generator $\mu_p$ to $e_n$. This is independent of the positive chart and is a continuous generator section of the orientation local system. Use the same $e_n$ for all manifolds being compared.

If $F$ is smooth near $p$, $F(p)=q$, and $dF_p$ is invertible, its induced map on local integral homology carries $\mu_p$ to $\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)\mu_q$. In dimension zero put $e_0=[\mathrm{point}]$; the smooth sign $\varepsilon(p)$ gives $\mu_p=\varepsilon(p)[p]$, and the local multiplier is the product of the source and target point signs. All assertions are choice-free. The local map is formed on a sufficiently small neighbourhood on which $p$ is the only preimage of $q$.

Let $F:M^n\to N^n$ be a smooth map of oriented smooth manifolds, and let $p$ be a regular preimage of $y$, so $F(p)=y$ and $dF_p:T_pM\to T_yN$ is an isomorphism. The **local orientation sign** $\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)$ is $+1$ if the induced isomorphism of determinant lines carries the chosen ray of $T_pM$ to the chosen ray of $T_yN$, and $-1$ if it carries it to the other ray. For $n>0$ it is the sign of the derivative determinant in positively oriented bases. For $n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_M(p)\varepsilon_N(y)$, comparing the two specified rays directly; it need not be $+1$, although the empty determinant is one.

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a diffeomorphism of oriented smooth $n$-manifolds and
$\omega\in\Omega_c^n(N)$. If $F$ preserves orientation everywhere,
$\int_MF^*\omega=\int_N\omega$; if it reverses orientation everywhere,
$\int_MF^*\omega=-\int_N\omega$. If the sign varies between components,
apply the appropriate signed equality on each component and add. The
compact-support integrals are the choice-free finite-chart values, equal to
the global partition integrals whenever those are available.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

analytic and cohomological suppliers invoked by the results below assume full
AC, and each item records its exact use. The definitional content below uses no

**(1) Compact Kähler manifolds.** Let $n\ge1$. A **Kähler manifold** is a complex
manifold $X$ of complex dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with complex structure
$J$ and a **Hermitian metric** $g$ — a Riemannian metric
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$ — whose **real fundamental form**
$\omega(v,w)=g(Jv,w)$ is

- a smooth real 2-form, the section of $\Lambda^2T^*X$ obtained by alternating
  $g(J\cdot,\cdot)$;
- **positive**: $\omega(v,Jv)=g(Jv,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v$;
- **closed**: $d\omega=0$.

The manifold is **compact Kähler** when the topological space $X$ is compact.

**Orientation.** For a complex basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of a tangent space $T_xX$,
the ordered real basis $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_n,Jv_n)$ is declared **positive**. This
is well defined: two complex bases differ by a complex-linear automorphism, whose
real determinant is the square of the modulus of its complex determinant and so
is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$ and $g(v_j,Jv_k)=0$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a real-linear endomorphism
of $V_{\mathbb R}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. It need not preserve $V$.

form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

$J:V\to V$ be a compatible complex structure ($J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all $v,w$). Let $\omega\in\bigwedge^2V$ satisfy
$\omega(v,w)=-g(Jv,w)$ for all $v,w$, and orient $V$ so that $\omega^n/n!$ is a
positive volume form. These are the form-side conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]: $V$ is the
cotangent space at a point, $J$ acts on forms by pullback, and $\omega$ is the
fundamental form. Write $h$ for the induced determinant pairing on the complexified exterior
algebra $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, extended sesquilinearly from $g$
with distinct degrees orthogonal and conjugate-linearity in the second variable, put $L=\omega\wedge$, let $\Lambda=L^*$ be the adjoint
with respect to $h$, and put $H=[L,\Lambda]$ and
$W=\exp L\exp(-\Lambda)\exp L$. Degrees of exterior powers below range over $0\le k\le2n$ (exterior powers
outside this range are zero). Let $J$ also denote the algebra endomorphism
$J(x\wedge y)=Jx\wedge Jy$ of $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, let
$\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$ be the span of $p$-fold wedges of
$V^{1,0}=\ker(J-i)$ with $q$-fold wedges of $V^{0,1}=\ker(J+i)$, and let $*$ be
the complex-linear extension of the Hodge star of $V$ and
$\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

   $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$, $[H,L]=2L$ and $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$.
2. Every $\alpha\in\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ has a unique decomposition
   $\alpha=\sum_{r\ge\max(0,k-n)}L^ru_r$ with $\Lambda u_r=0$ and
   $u_r\in\bigwedge^{k-2r}V_{\mathbb C}$; all but finitely many terms vanish,
   and the projections $\alpha\mapsto u_r$ are rational polynomials in
   $L,\Lambda$ on each fixed degree.
3. If $0\le t\le n$ and $u\in\bigwedge^tV_{\mathbb C}$ is primitive
   ($\Lambda u=0$) of degree $t$,
   then $L^{n-t+1}u=0$ and
   $$\Lambda^sL^ru=\frac{r!}{(r-s)!}\frac{(n-t-r+s)!}{(n-t-r)!}L^{r-s}u\qquad(0\le s\le r\le n-t);$$
   no nonzero primitive element has degree $t>n$; for $k\le n$ an element of
   $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ is primitive exactly when $L^{n-k+1}u=0$; and
   $L^{n-k}:\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^{2n-k}V_{\mathbb C}$ is an
   isomorphism for $k\le n$.
4. $J=i^{p-q}$ on $\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$, and
   $W\alpha=\epsilon(k)J*\alpha$ for every $\alpha$ of degree $k$. If $0\le k=p+q\le n$ and $u$ is
   primitive of type $(p,q)$, then
   $$*u=\frac{\epsilon(k)i^{q-p}}{(n-k)!}L^{n-k}u .$$

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary,
$\mu$ a smooth positive density on $M$, and $E,F\to M$ finite-rank smooth vector
bundles over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ with smooth bundle metrics,
Hermitian (first-variable-linear) in the complex case, with the conventions of
[[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]. Let
$P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(F)$ be a linear differential operator of order at most two
(the target-$F$ version of the local description in
[[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]).

Then there is a unique linear differential operator $P^\star:\Gamma(F)\to\Gamma(E)$
of order at most two such that
$$\int_M\langle Pu,v\rangle_F\,d\mu=\int_M\langle u,P^\star v\rangle_E\,d\mu$$
for all compactly supported smooth sections $u\in\Gamma_c(E)$ and
$v\in\Gamma_c(F)$; it is the **formal adjoint** of $P$. It is given locally as
follows: in a chart with coordinates $x$, with density coefficient $\gamma>0$
defined by $\mu=\gamma\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$
([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]), with frames of $E$ and $F$
orthonormal for the metrics (equivalently unitary in the complex case; such
frames exist locally by applying Gram–Schmidt to any local frame,
[[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]), and with local coefficients
$Pu=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}a_\alpha D^\alpha u$,
$$P^\star v=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}(-1)^{|\alpha|}\gamma^{-1}D^\alpha\bigl(\gamma\,a_\alpha^*v\bigr),$$
where $a_\alpha^*$ is the fibre adjoint. Consequently:
1. if the leading coefficients of $P$ of order $\delta\in\{0,1,2\}$ are the
   matrices $a_\alpha$, $|\alpha|=\delta$, then those of $P^\star$ are
   $(-1)^\delta a_\alpha^*$, computed in the same orthonormal frames; in
   particular the formal adjoint of a Laplace-type operator is again Laplace
   type and its principal symbol is unchanged,
   $\sigma_2(P^\star)=\sigma_2(P)$;
2. $(P^\star)^\star=P$;
3. if $E=F$, then $P$ is formally symmetric in the sense of
   [[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]] exactly when
   $P=P^\star$.

- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open and let all forms below be smooth and
complex-valued. Then
$$d=\partial+\bar\partial,\qquad \partial^2=0,\qquad \bar\partial^2=0,\qquad \partial\bar\partial+\bar\partial\partial=0.$$
For $\eta\in\Omega^{p,q}(U)$ and $\theta\in\Omega^{r,s}(U)$,
$$\partial(\eta\wedge\theta)=\partial\eta\wedge\theta+(-1)^{p+q}\eta\wedge\partial\theta,\qquad \bar\partial(\eta\wedge\theta)=\bar\partial\eta\wedge\theta+(-1)^{p+q}\eta\wedge\bar\partial\theta.$$
The identities hold at bidegree endpoints as well, with components outside
$0\le p,q\le n$ interpreted as zero.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

derivations.claim: For $n\ge1$, fix $x_0\in X$ and choose holomorphic coordinates with $h_{a\bar b}(0)=\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$, where $h_{a\bar b}=g_{\mathbb C}(\partial_{z_a},\partial_{\bar z_b})$ for the complex-bilinear extension of $g$. Then $\omega=i\sum_{a,b}h_{a\bar b}\,dz_a\wedge d\bar z_b$, and $d\omega=0$ implies $\partial_ch_{a\bar b}=\partial_ah_{c\bar b}$. Put $\Gamma^b_{ac}=2\partial_ah_{c\bar b}(0)$ and make the symmetric quadratic change $z_b=w_b-\tfrac12\sum_{a,c}\Gamma^b_{ac}w_aw_c$. Its derivative at zero is the identity, so [F4] makes it a holomorphic coordinate change near zero. In the transformed matrix $h'_{a\bar b}=\sum_{i,j}h_{i\bar j}(z(w))(\partial z_i/\partial w_a)\overline{(\partial z_j/\partial w_b)}$, one has $\partial_ch'_{a\bar b}(0)=\partial_ch_{a\bar b}(0)-\tfrac12\Gamma^b_{ac}=0$. The antiholomorphic derivatives vanish by the Hermitian symmetry. Thus $h'=\tfrac12 I+O(|w|^2)$, and the induced form metric, its inverse and the volume density have vanishing first derivatives at zero. Formula [F2] therefore gives the flat adjoint formulas at this point. When $n=0$ the claimed identities are immediate from [F1]; assume $n\ge1$ below.

Work at such a normal point with the constant-coefficient operators on the coframe $dz_j,d\bar z_j$: write $a_j=dz_j\wedge$, $b_j=d\bar z_j\wedge$ and let $c_j=a_j^*$, $d_j=b_j^*$ be the pointwise adjoints of [F1], so that $\{c_j,a_k\}=2\delta_{jk}$, $\{d_j,b_k\}=2\delta_{jk}$ and the mixed anticommutators $\{c_j,b_k\}$, $\{d_j,a_k\}$ vanish (the factor two is $h(dz_j,dz_j)$). Then $\partial=\sum_ja_j\partial_{z_j}$, $\bar\partial=\sum_jb_j\partial_{\bar z_j}$, $\partial^*=-\sum_jc_j\partial_{\bar z_j}$, $\bar\partial^*=-\sum_jd_j\partial_{z_j}$, $L=\frac i2\sum_ja_jb_j$ and $\Lambda=-\frac i2\sum_jd_jc_j$, and direct expansion using the anticommutation relations gives $\Lambda\partial-\partial\Lambda=-i\sum_jd_j\partial_{z_j}=i\bar\partial^*$ (the mixed pairs $[d_jc_j,a_k]=2\delta_{jk}d_j$), $\Lambda\bar\partial-\bar\partial\Lambda=i\sum_jc_j\partial_{\bar z_j}=-i\partial^*$, $\bar\partial^*L-L\bar\partial^*=i\sum_ja_j\partial_{z_j}=i\partial$ and $\partial^*L-L\partial^*=-i\sum_jb_j\partial_{\bar z_j}=-i\bar\partial$. Every one of these operators is a differential operator of order at most two whose coefficients involve at most first derivatives of the metric, so equality at every normal point proves the four identities globally; the normalization enters only through the factor $h(dz_j,dz_j)=2$, and both sides scale the same way if the metric is rescaled by a constant, so no normalization is mixed inside the computation.

Use the graded bracket, for which the bracket of two odd operators is their anticommutator and $[\Lambda,\partial]=i\bar\partial^*$ reads $\bar\partial^*=-i[\Lambda,\partial]$. By [F3] the operators $\partial,\bar\partial$ are odd and satisfy $\partial^2=\bar\partial^2=\partial\bar\partial+\bar\partial\partial=0$, while $\Lambda$ is even. Graded Jacobi applied to $\partial,\Lambda,\partial$ gives $[\partial,[\Lambda,\partial]]=0$ because the two middle terms cancel and $\partial^2=0$, hence $[\partial,\bar\partial^*]=-i[\partial,[\Lambda,\partial]]=0$, and its adjoint gives $[\bar\partial,\partial^*]=0$; these are exactly the two vanishing mixed anticommutators. Graded Jacobi applied to $\bar\partial,\Lambda,\partial$ gives $[\bar\partial,[\Lambda,\partial]]=[\partial,[\bar\partial,\Lambda]]$, hence $[\bar\partial,\bar\partial^*]=-i[\bar\partial,[\Lambda,\partial]]=-i[\partial,[\bar\partial,\Lambda]]=i[\partial,[\Lambda,\bar\partial]]=[\partial,\partial^*]$, using the second identity of step 2.1; that is $\Delta_{\bar\partial}=\Delta_\partial$. Expanding $d=\partial+\bar\partial$ and $d^*=\partial^*+\bar\partial^*$ with the two mixed anticommutators gives $\Delta_d=\Delta_\partial+\Delta_{\bar\partial}=2\Delta_\partial=2\Delta_{\bar\partial}$.

For the remaining commutation relations: $[\partial,L]=\partial\omega\wedge=0$ and $[\bar\partial,L]=0$ by [F3]; then $[\Delta_\partial,L]=\partial[\partial^*,L]+[\partial,L]\partial^*+[\partial^*,L]\partial+\partial^*[\partial,L]=-i(\partial\bar\partial+\bar\partial\partial)=0$, where the first equality uses $\Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial$ and $[\partial^*,L]=-i\bar\partial$, and adjunction gives $[\Delta_\partial,\Lambda]=0$; since $\Delta_d=2\Delta_\partial$, $\Delta_d$ commutes with $L$ and $\Lambda$. Commutation with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ follows from $\partial^2=\bar\partial^2=0$ and $\Delta_d=2\Delta_\partial=2\Delta_{\bar\partial}$. For the star: for $\alpha$ of degree $k-1$ and $\beta$ of degree $k$ the formal-adjoint identity of [F2] for $d$ and the characterizing property $\alpha'\wedge*\bar\beta=\langle\alpha',\beta\rangle\,dV$ of the star give $\int\alpha\wedge*\overline{d^*\beta}=(-1)^k\int\alpha\wedge d*\bar\beta$, hence, since this holds for all $\alpha$, the operator identity $*d^*=(-1)^kd*$ on degree $k$; substituting it and $*^2=(-1)^{k(m-k)}$ with $m=2n$ into $\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d$ shows $*\Delta_d=\Delta_d*$ on every degree, because the adjacent-degree relations are $*d^*=(-1)^k d*$ and $*d=(-1)^{k+1}d^**$ on degree $k$, and hence $*dd^*=d^*d*$ and $*d^*d=dd^**$. Finally $\Delta_{\bar\partial}=\Delta_d/2$ has bidegree $(0,0)$ because $\bar\partial$ and $\bar\partial^*$ shift bidegree by $(0,\pm1)$, so $\Delta_d$ preserves each $\Omega^{p,q}(X)$. For $n=0$ every operator but the star is zero and all assertions are immediate.

citations.quote:
In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For a CW complex $X$ and abelian group $G$, set $C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)=H_n(X^n,X^{n-1};G)$ and $C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)=0$ for $n<0$. By [[thm-relative-homology-of-consecutive-cw-skeleta]], an orientation of each characteristic $n$-disk selects the corresponding direct-summand copy of $G$.

Let $X$ be a CW complex, $G$ an abelian group, and $n\geq0$.
The **cellular homology** of $X$ with coefficients in $G$ is
$H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)=\ker d_n/\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$ for the cellular
groups of [[def-oriented-cellular-chain-group]], with differentials defined in
[[def-cellular-boundary-from-three-consecutive-skeleta]].  These maps form a
chain complex by [[lem-the-cellular-boundary-squares-to-zero]].

Let $X$ be a topological space. For each integer $n\geq 0$, a
**singular $n$-simplex in $X$** is a continuous map
$$\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$$
from the standard topological simplex of
[[def-standard-topological-simplex-and-its-affine-face-maps]]. Write
$S_n(X)$ for the set of all singular $n$-simplices in $X$.

The **singular chain group with integer coefficients** is the free abelian group
on $S_n(X)$:
$$C_n(X;\mathbb Z):=\bigoplus_{\sigma\in S_n(X)}\mathbb Z[\sigma].$$
Thus an element of $C_n(X;\mathbb Z)$ is a finite formal sum
$$\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\sigma_k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,\ \sigma_k\in S_n(X).$$

If $G$ is an abelian group, the **singular chain group with coefficients in
$G$** is
$$C_n(X;G):=C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z} G,$$
using the tensor product of
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]. The page's
convention is that coefficients are attached through this tensor-product
construction, not by choosing a preferred $G$-basis of singular simplices.

Let $X$ be any topological space and $G$ an abelian group. Its **singular cochains with coefficients in $G$** are
$$C^n(X;G)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(C_n(X;\mathbb Z),G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad C^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0),$$
where the chains are those of [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. Addition and negatives of homomorphisms are pointwise. The **coboundary** is
$$\delta^n:C^n(X;G)\to C^{n+1}(X;G),\qquad \delta^n\varphi=\varphi\circ\partial_{n+1}$$
for $n\ge0$, and is zero for $n<0$. Composition with the homomorphism [[def-singular-boundary-operator|$\partial_{n+1}$]] is additive, so this is a homomorphism. The sign convention is positive: there is no extra degree sign on this composite. On a singular $(n+1)$-simplex it says
$$\delta^n\varphi(\sigma)=\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\circ\delta_i),$$
where $\delta_i$ denotes the affine face map, distinct from the superscripted coboundary. In particular $\delta^0\varphi$ on an oriented path is its endpoint value minus its initial value.

By [[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]], the integer chains are finite sums on the specified simplex set $S_n(X)$. Thus a cochain is equivalently an arbitrary function $S_n(X)\to G$: the extension sends $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ to $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$. The sum is finite and the formal coefficients are unique. The cochain need not have finite support.

For a commutative unital ring $R$ and an $R$-module $G$, there is a canonical identification
$$C^n(X;G)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_n(X;R),G).$$
Indeed the given chain convention is $C_n(X;R)=C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R$. A homomorphism $\varphi$ on integer chains defines an $R$-linear map by $c\otimes r\mapsto r\varphi(c)$; the defining additive and integer-balanced tensor relations are preserved. Conversely evaluate an $R$-linear map on $c\otimes1$. These operations are inverse since $c\otimes r=r(c\otimes1)$, and they intertwine the two coboundaries because the coefficient boundary is $\partial\otimes1$. The construction also covers the zero ring with its unital zero module.

The resulting graded group and coboundary are called the **singular cochain complex**. The square-zero identity follows by precomposition with $\partial^2=0$ in the chain complex and is spelled out in the next lemma. If $X$ is empty there are no singular simplices, so every cochain group is zero; if $G=0$ the same is true. The extension and tensor formulas are uniquely specified and require no AC.

For a space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, a degree-$n$ **singular cocycle** is a cochain in $Z^n(X;G)=\ker\delta^n$ and a degree-$n$ **singular coboundary** belongs to $B^n(X;G)=\operatorname{im}\delta^{n-1}$, for the positive coboundary convention of [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. The square-zero lemma [[lem-the-singular-coboundary-squares-to-zero]] implies $B^n\subseteq Z^n$: if $\varphi=\delta^{n-1}\psi$, then $\delta^n\varphi=0$.

The **singular cohomology group with coefficients in $G$** is
$$H^n(X;G)=Z^n(X;G)/B^n(X;G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad H^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0).$$
This is the abelian quotient with addition $[\varphi]+[\psi]=[\varphi+\psi]$: changing either representative by a coboundary changes the sum by a coboundary. Thus two cocycles represent the same class exactly when their difference is $\delta^{n-1}\eta$ for some degree-$(n-1)$ cochain $\eta$. In degree zero, $B^0=0$ because $C^{-1}=0$; hence $H^0=\ker\delta^0$. The zero convention in negative degrees agrees with the same kernel/image construction on the zero cochain groups.

If coefficients are a module over a commutative ring, the same groups and maps are modules and linear maps, and this is their module quotient. Empty $X$ or zero coefficients give zero cohomology in every degree. The notation does not define cohomology as the dual of homology; such identifications require their own theorems. No choice of cocycle representatives and no AC is part of this definition.

Let $M$ be a right $R$-module, let ${}_RN_S$ be an $(R,S)$-bimodule, and let $P$ be a left $S$-module. There is a canonical group isomorphism

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}:(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\longrightarrow M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$$

determined by

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}((m\otimes n)\otimes p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$

It respects any compatible outer module actions and is natural in $M,N,P$.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

Let $X$ be a space, let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, and use the positive coboundary $\delta\varphi=\varphi\partial$ of [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. For $p,q\ge0$ and cochains $\varphi\in C^p(X;R)$, $\psi\in C^q(X;R)$, their **cup product** is
$$(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)=\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p])\,\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\qquad(\sigma:\Delta^{p+q}\to X).$$
Extend from simplex generators $R$-linearly. The product is $R$-bilinear in the cochains by distributivity and commutativity in $R$. Zero or negative-degree inputs give zero.

With $J(\varphi,\psi)$ the tensor functional of [[def-additive-singular-cohomology-cross-product]] and $A=\operatorname{AW}$ from [[def-alexander-whitney-diagonal-approximation]], this is exactly $J(\varphi,\psi)A\Delta_\#$. Indeed only the cut of bidegree $(p,q)$ survives. Equivalently, define the AW external **cochain** by $J(\varphi,\psi)A$ and pull it back along the diagonal. There is no extra cochain sign.

The earlier additive **cohomology** cross product was expressed through a specified shuffle inverse $T$. The comparison with it is an equality of classes: [[thm-alexander-whitney-and-eilenberg-zilber-are-chain-homotopy-inverses]] constructs $K$ with $A-T=dK+Kd$. For cocycles, [[lem-additive-singular-cohomology-cross-product-is-well-defined]] gives $Jd=0$, hence
$$J(A-T)\Delta_\#=JKd\Delta_\#=\delta(JK\Delta_\#).$$
Here postcomposition with the diagonal commutes with boundary, as proved in the diagonal definition. Thus the AW cup class equals diagonal pullback of the earlier external product; equality of the two chosen external cochains is not required. At total degree zero the displayed primitive is zero and the identity is literal. The same tensor-functional identity gives $\delta(JA\Delta_\#)=0$ for cocycles, so the compared classes exist.

For degree-zero cochains the formula on a vertex is ordinary multiplication of their values. A constant cochain of value $1$ multiplies any cochain on either side without changing it, including on disconnected spaces. On empty $X$ or over $R=0$ all cochains and products are zero. Face restrictions make sense for every singular simplex, including degenerate ones. A bare abelian coefficient group has no specified multiplication to insert in this formula. No AC or selection of representatives is used in this definition or comparison.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$ and a commutative unital ring $R$, pullback on singular cohomology satisfies
$$f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b,\qquad f^*(1)=1.$$
Cup product is associative already on cochains. Consequently $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a unital graded-ring homomorphism. Homotopic maps give the same homomorphism.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] there are a finite CW complex $K$ and maps $h:X\to K$, $g:K\to X$ with $g\circ h$ homotopic to $\mathrm{id}_X$ and $h\circ g$ homotopic to $\mathrm{id}_K$. Homotopy invariance [F2] gives $g_*h_*=(g\circ h)_*=\mathrm{id}$ and $h_*g_*=(h\circ g)_*=\mathrm{id}$ on singular homology with any coefficients, so $h_*:H_n(X;\kappa)\to H_n(K;\kappa)$ is an isomorphism for every $n$ and every coefficient field $\kappa$. For a field $\kappa$ each cellular chain group $C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(K;\kappa)$ is a direct sum of one copy of $\kappa$ per $n$-cell [F3], and the finite CW complex $K$ has finitely many cells, so $C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(K;\kappa)$ is a finite-dimensional $\kappa$-vector space and its subquotient $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(K;\kappa)=\ker d_n/\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$ is finite-dimensional as well [F3]; by cellular homology equals singular homology [F3], $H_n(K;\kappa)$ and hence $H_n(X;\kappa)$ are finite-dimensional. In particular $H_n(X;\mathbb Q)$ and $H_n(X;\mathbb R)$ are finite-dimensional for every $n$.

Let $k$ be a field, let $F$ be a $k$-vector space, and let $D_*$ be a chain complex of $k$-vector spaces with differential $\partial$, cycles $Z_n=\ker\partial_n$ and boundaries $B_n=\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$. Under AC choose $k$-linear complements $A_n,T_n$ with $Z_n=B_n\oplus A_n$ and $D_n=Z_n\oplus T_n$; then $\partial_n$ maps $T_n$ isomorphically onto $B_{n-1}$, because it is injective ($T_n\cap Z_n=0$) and $\partial_n(D_n)=B_{n-1}=\partial_n(T_n)$. Tensoring these supplied splittings preserves them: tensor the inclusions and projections, whose composites are identities or zero and whose sum is the identity. Thus $D_n\otimes_kF=(B_n\otimes_kF)\oplus(A_n\otimes_kF)\oplus(T_n\otimes_kF)$, and the boundary is zero on the first two summands and an isomorphism from the third onto $B_{n-1}\otimes_kF$. Consequently $\ker(\partial_n\otimes1)=Z_n\otimes_kF$, $\operatorname{im}(\partial_{n+1}\otimes1)=B_n\otimes_kF$, and $H_n(D_*\otimes_kF)\cong A_n\otimes_kF\cong H_n(D_*)\otimes_kF$, the isomorphism sending the class of $z\otimes\mu$ to $[z]\otimes\mu$. For $D_*=C_*(X;\mathbb Q)$ and $k=\mathbb Q$ the chain-level identification $C_*(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong C_*(X;F)$ is the associativity and unit isomorphism for $C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}F$ [F4], so $H_n(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong H_n(X;F)$ canonically by the map induced by $c\mapsto c\otimes1$.

Fix a characteristic-zero field $F$ and a degree $n$, and put $V=H_n(X;\mathbb Q)$, finite-dimensional by step 1.1. Evaluation gives natural isomorphisms $H^n(X;\kappa)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_\kappa(H_n(X;\kappa),\kappa)$ for $\kappa=\mathbb Q$ and $\kappa=F$ [F5]; choosing a finite $\mathbb Q$-basis $(v_i)$ of the finite-dimensional space $V$ with dual basis $(f_i)$, the map $f_i\otimes\mu\mapsto(v_j\mapsto\delta_{ij}\mu)$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(V,\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(V,F)$, and $\psi\mapsto(v\otimes\mu\mapsto\psi(v)\mu)$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(V,F)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_F(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F,F)$, with inverse $\chi\mapsto(v\mapsto\chi(v\otimes1))$. Composing these isomorphisms with the identification $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong H_n(X;F)$ of step 1.2 and the two evaluation isomorphisms gives a natural isomorphism $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong H^n(X;F)$; on a cocycle $\varphi$ and a chain $z\otimes\mu$ the image of $[\varphi]\otimes1$ evaluates to $\varphi(z)\mu$, exactly as the coefficient-change cochain $c\otimes\mu\mapsto\varphi(c)\mu$ does, so the isomorphism is the natural coefficient map $[\varphi]\otimes1\mapsto[\varphi\otimes1]$. Hence $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong H^n(X;F)$ for every characteristic-zero field $F$, and $H^n(X;F)$ is finite-dimensional because $H_n(X;F)\cong V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F$ is.

By [F6] the cup product on singular cochains with coefficients in a commutative unital ring is given by the front/back formula, and the coefficient-change map $\varphi\mapsto\varphi\otimes1$ satisfies $((\varphi\smile\psi)\otimes1)(\sigma)=(\varphi\otimes1)(\sigma[0,\dots,p])\cdot(\psi\otimes1)(\sigma[p,\dots,p+q])$ on every singular simplex by multiplying the two coefficient values inside $F$, with $1\otimes1=1$; hence coefficient change is a unital homomorphism of graded rings, and the isomorphism of step 2.1, being its $F$-linear extension, satisfies $\Phi_F((a\smile b)\otimes\mu)=\Phi_F(a\otimes1)\smile\Phi_F(b\otimes\mu)$ for cohomology classes $a,b$ and scalars $\mu$, so the comparison isomorphisms preserve cup products. For a map $f:X\to Y$ of compact smooth manifolds the cochain identity $f^*(\varphi\otimes1)=(f^*\varphi)\otimes1$ holds because both sides send a simplex $\sigma$ to $\varphi(f\circ\sigma)$, and pullback is a unital graded-ring homomorphism [F6]; hence the isomorphisms of step 2.1 commute with pullback and are natural for such maps, and multiplicativity is preserved as well.

The de Rham theorem [F7] gives the natural isomorphism of graded real algebras $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)\cong H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathbb R)$, so composing with step 2.1 for $F=\mathbb R$ identifies $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ with real de Rham cohomology; the real de Rham theorem assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, which AC supplies through [F1]. For $F=\mathbb C$ the complex de Rham complex is $\Omega^*_{\mathbb R}(X)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ with differential $d\otimes1$ [F7], and the argument of step 1.2 applied degreewise to this complex over the field extension $\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb C$ gives $H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X;\mathbb C)\cong H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(X;\mathbb R)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$; likewise $H^n(X;\mathbb C)\cong H^n(X;\mathbb R)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$, either by the same base change and duality [F5] or by associativity from $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\cong H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ via step 2.1 for $F=\mathbb R$ and $F=\mathbb C$. Hence the complex de Rham comparison is the complexification of the real one, and the identification with real or complex de Rham cohomology holds for $F=\mathbb R,\mathbb C$ as asserted, with naturality and cup-product compatibility from steps 2.1 and 3.1.
